title.en: Purim, a day of the World to Come in disguise

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens that Purim is a day of the World to Come dressed in this world, like the whole Megillah. He speaks of the different ways of tzaddikim at the Purim tish and says Purim is a time to ask Hashem for emunah, warm tefillos and every good thing.

title.en: Moshe's birth in Adar and the fiftieth gate

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Haman, who knew Moshe died in Adar, did not know he was also born then. He explains that on the day of his passing Moshe attained the fiftieth gate, hinted in 'Har Nevo', while Haman built a gallows of fifty amos to reach the fiftieth gate of impurity. He brings the Tomer Devorah on the highest level where no accuser reaches.

title.en: 'Today I have born you' and asking on Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Purim a Jew connects to that highest world and becomes a new birth, 'ani hayom yelidticha', and therefore can ask, as Esther asked for her soul and her people. He connects Purim to Moshe through Mordechai and 'kiymu v'kiblu', and brings that 'ad d'lo yada' equals the seventh of Adar when Moshe was born.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Singing.

title.en: The holiness of Keser all day

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that the holiness of Keser said in Shabbos Musaf rests on Purim the whole day, and that the word 'Keser' appears in Tanach only in the Megillah. On Yom Kippur one must rise to Hashem; on Purim Hashem comes down to the lowest level.

title.en: Why Achashverosh's feast had no instruments

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Maharal's question why the Megillah does not mention musical instruments at Achashverosh's feast. He explains the link of instruments to this world through Yuval and his brother Tuval-Kayin and their sister Naamah, and that Achashverosh wanted to show he had a Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: Yerushalayim and the song of the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that tonight one connects to Yerushalayim. Shabbos and the future are above instruments, so Achashverosh, imitating the future Beis Hamikdash, had none. He ends with the close of Tehillim, where above all the instruments 'kol haneshamah' praises Hashem, and calls on all to sing with the soul.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Singing.

title.en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara on where one begins reading the Megillah and asks why Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's view, to begin from 'that night', appears only in a Baraisa. He explains that Rashbi is a soul for whom there is no churban, tells of the Satmar Rav in Meron, and distinguishes the Megillah's story from its hidden meaning.

title.en: Shushan Purim and the wall of fire

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Avnei Nezer that the five days of reading the Megillah match the five final letters, each a redemption, so Shushan Purim in Yerushalayim matches the final redemption. He links it to 'a wall of fire around' and the gematria of 'that night the king's sleep was disturbed', and asks for a niggun.

title.en: Modeh Ani and the hidden root of a Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Modeh Ani may be said before washing: it has no Name of Hashem, and the point of a Jew it expresses cannot be defiled. This is the point of Avraham Avinu, the hidden root, which Hashem guards. The Megillah, too, is this point and this 'reishis'.

title.en: Keser reaches the last; Hashem is near

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that the 'reishis' of Keser joins with the 'acharis': Adar, Shushan in Eilam, and the lowest Jew, so even then a Jew says Modeh Ani and feels both how far and how near he is. He brings Rav Masna's opening to the Megillah, 'G-d is close to it', which needs no key, and says perhaps today is the last day of galus.

title.en: Purim as a covenant, and the two goats

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen that Purim is a covenant between Hashem and Israel from the hidden root, that even in sin a Jew is attached to Hashem. He explains the two identical goats of Yom Kippur chosen by lot, Esav and Yaakov, 'I love Yaakov', and that Purim too came by a lot.

title.en: Rashbi, the shoshanah and the garments of Esav

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Purim falls on the same weekday as Lag BaOmer and explains that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai revealed the secret of every Jew. Esther is a rose among thorns, Yaakov received the brachos in Esav's garments, and 'his garments' are read as 'his traitors'; Purim is the time for every Jew to find his hidden root.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Singing.

title.en: Mordechai grabbed Adar

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the months were divided between Yaakov and Esav and that Yaakov grabbed Elul, while Mordechai, from Binyamin, grabbed Adar. He brings the episode at the end of Shoftim where the tribe of Binyamin was told to 'grab' wives at Shiloh.

title.en: Purim, a day of grabbing

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the one woman of Binyamin who grabbed her husband, the mother of Shaul, from whom came Shaul, Mordechai and Esther. He brings 'Binyamin is a wolf that tears' and Rashi, and calls on every Jew to grab: to grab malchus, to grab hold of Hashem and come close to the King.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude in the seudah.

title.en: Haman's generosity and Timna

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks where Haman, of a stingy klipah, got the generosity to give ten thousand talents of silver. He answers that Haman descends from Timna, who wanted to join Avraham Avinu and was refused; her good will went down to Amalek and Haman, and the verse about her equals the ten thousand talents in gematria.

title.en: Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Yismach Moshe on the Gemara that Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak: the Jews did not touch the spoil because the 'spoil' was holy souls within Amalek. He adds from the Tefillas Shlomo that Haman merited this by eating at Esther's holy feast, with a gematria on 'let the king and Haman come today to the feast'.

title.en: Krias Shema and the Tannaim in Bnei Brak

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Zeresh advised hanging Mordechai in the morning so he could not say Krias Shema. Timna wanted to join Avraham to be able to say 'Shema Yisrael', and Haman's descendants in Bnei Brak could not say it, until the Tannaim reclining in Bnei Brak on Pesach night rectified them.

title.en: The late soul and the Megillah on Pesach night

summary.en: The Mashgiach relates the Spinka Rebbe's story of a late soul that received its tikkun when a young man, the Imrei Yosef himself, read the Megillah on the second night of Pesach and ruled that it is Purim. In the same way the Tannaim in Bnei Brak rectified Haman's descendants by reading the Megillah on Pesach night, and today everyone can accept the yoke of Heaven and reveal Timna's hidden will.

title.en: The ben sorer u'moreh: no Jew is beyond hope

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah writes the ben sorer u'moreh if it never was and never will be, since whatever is in the Torah exists in the world. He answers that a Jewish soul is a part of G-d above and no one can rule that a Jew has no more hope; the Torah's conditions make it impossible, teaching that any Jew can become a tzaddik.

title.en: The heart, Chevron and Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'my heart says to You, seek My face' with Rashi: the heart is Hashem's messenger in the soul. In place it is Chevron, the Cave of the Patriarchs, which was never destroyed; in time it is Purim, 'I shall surely hide', the point that can never be nullified, even after Achashverosh's feast.

title.en: Magen Avraham and the Jew who drinks on Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chiddushei HaRim that Hashem guards the point of Avraham, with gematrios on 'the days of Mordechai and Esther' and 'Your faithfulness in the nights'. Purim will never be nullified. On Purim a Jew who eats meat and drinks wine says to Hashem: look at me, I am a zolel v'sovei, but I have a hidden root, and even the ben sorer u'moreh can become a man.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Singing.

title.en: The man who nursed his child, and Mordechai

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara of the man whose wife died and for whom a miracle was made so he could nurse his infant; Rav Yosef said 'how great', Abaye 'how lowly'. The Midrash says Mordechai too nursed Esther, and he asks how one can say 'lowly' of Mordechai; he finds the Tosafos Yeshanim's answer difficult.

title.en: Rebbe's mother, the queen and Antoninus

summary.en: The Mashgiach relates from Tosafos how Rebbe's mother circumcised him despite the Roman decree, and the queen, who loved her, exchanged infants so the king saw an uncircumcised child. Antoninus nursed from Rebbe's mother and later converted. He asks how Rebbe could nurse from the queen, and begins to answer through 'shnayim mikra v'echad targum'.

title.en: The Megillah goes down into Targum

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that fallen souls are in the realm of Targum, and the Megillah, which has more Targum than any other sefer, goes down to raise them; Mordechai's name itself is Targum. Haman said the Jews 'sleep', and the salvation came when 'the King's sleep' was disturbed. Timna is gematria 'shnayim mikra v'echad targum', and Rav Yosef is the soul that rectifies Targum.

title.en: Tzafnas Paneach and milk without the left side

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yosef's two sons match the two Adars and that his Targum name, Tzafnas Paneach, hints at Mordechai and at drinking on Purim. Purim is Keser, where there is no left side, so Esther had to nurse from a male, and a miracle was made for Mordechai; the man in the Gemara was a gilgul of Mordechai, which is why Rav Yosef said 'how great'.

title.en: Yaakov and Esav: Rebbe, Antoninus and the queen

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from seforim that Rebbe was a gilgul of Yaakov and Antoninus of Esav, so the queen and Rebbe's mother were each like Rivkah nursing both; the queen was no simple soul and risked her life. He brings the Midrash that Haman told Mordechai his grandfather Yaakov bowed to Esav, and asks why Mordechai's answer suffices.

title.en: Bowing to the Shechinah, and the writing of the Mishnah

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that Yaakov bowed to the Shechinah that passed before him, as 'ish Yehudi' contains Hashem's Name. He explains that Rebbe needed the queen's milk for writing down the Mishnah, an 'eis la'asos' that permitted what is otherwise forbidden, and connects this to Mordechai nursing Esther.

title.en: The wine of Purim and Torah after chatzos

summary.en: As chatzos approaches, the Mashgiach speaks of the special wine of Purim and gives a brachah for bright Shabbosos, Yamim Tovim and learning. He mentions the Satmar Rav, who said he became drunk twice a year, and teaches that after chatzos Hashem learns Torah with the souls in Gan Eden, and on Purim it is a Torah of the merits of Jews.

title.en: Worth a lifetime to read the Megillah once

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that the Satmar Rav, after all he went through in Europe, said in America that it was worth everything to read the Megillah once. He blesses that the Megillah, the seudah, mishloach manos and matanos l'evyonim bring blessing for the whole year, and returns to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who found good in every Jew, and to Purim and Lag BaOmer.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that Purim reaches down to the lowest Jew, lifts the holy sparks hidden even in Haman, and binds the Jews of the farthest places to Yerushalayim and to the level of Keser.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a blessing for the gathering and explains that Purim reveals the hidden point of emunah in every Jew; the Megillah is a personal letter to the lowest soul. He then shows how holiness came from Amalek: Shaul left Agag alive one night, Yehoshua only weakened Amalek, and Haman carried a holy spark that came from Timna's longing to join the house of Avraham, a spark that later produced Rabbi Shmuel bar Shilas. Esther's request for an added day in Shushan links the lowest place, Shushan, with Yerushalayim, and Purim brings the light of Keser for a whole day. He connects the Gemara's teachings on cities near a walled city and on the letters mem-nun-tzadi-pei-chaf to souls who stand outside the walls yet long to be inside. He closes with the world of the golem, where everything can be overturned, and the wine of Purim.

en: Purim reveals the hidden point of emunah that every Jew carries, even the lowest soul of the generation before Moshiach.
The Megillah is an iggeres, a letter addressed personally to each Jew, down to the level of nefesh d'nefesh d'malchus d'asiyah.
Hashem wanted a remnant of Amalek to remain so that Haman, and through him Purim, would come into the world.
Haman carried a holy spark that came from Timna's longing to be brought close to Avraham Avinu, and from it came Rabbi Shmuel bar Shilas.
Through Esther's added day, Shushan, the lowest place, is joined to Yerushalayim, and Purim gives the light of Keser for a whole day.
Samuch v'nireh and the letters mem-nun-tzadi-pei-chaf both stand for souls outside the wall who long for Yerushalayim, and on Purim Hashem brings them inside.
The miracle of Purim comes from the world of the golem, where a decree can still be overturned, and Esther used it to turn Haman's two feasts into the Jews' two days of Purim.

title.en: Purim reveals the hidden point

summary.en: The Mashgiach blesses the gathering, says that any gathering of Jews may bring the salvation, and explains that on Purim the hidden point of emunah in every Jew is revealed, as the Jews then accepted the Torah anew.

title.en: The Megillah as a letter to the lowest Jew

summary.en: He brings the Tanya that even the lowest souls of the heel are bound to the head, and explains that the Megillah is an iggeres, a letter sent personally to each Jew; this point is why even the simplest Jews gave their lives for emunah.

title.en: Purim given in the deepest concealment

summary.en: He contrasts Achashveirosh's feast with Purim, which was given in hiding within hiding to the lowest Jews, compares this to the two goats of Yom Kippur that look alike, and ties the light of the Megillah to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's strength for even the weakest.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude.

title.en: Agag's night and the spark in Haman

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shaul left Agag alive and Yehoshua only weakened Amalek because Hashem wanted Haman to come. He brings the Arizal on blessing Haman when drunk and the Tiferes Shlomo that Haman left 'glad of heart' after eating Esther's holy seudah, which awakened the spark from which his descendants taught Torah in Bnei Brak.

title.en: Timna's longing and its fruit

summary.en: He asks where Haman got a holy spark and answers from the Gemara on 'and Lotan's sister was Timna': Timna longed to join Avraham's house and became a pilegesh to Eliphaz. That longing passed through Amalek and Haman to Rabbi Shmuel bar Shilas, the faithful melamed, once the time came to bring the distant close.

title.en: The Ruzhiner on Shaul, and targum

summary.en: He tells the Ruzhiner's explanation of Shaul's words 'I have fulfilled the word of Hashem', then explains that Timna's soul was at the level of targum, which had to wait to be refined, and that Agag sensed the descendant who would come from him.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude.

title.en: Esther's added day and Shushan

summary.en: He explains that Esther asked for an added day, and every addition draws down holiness; from it came the soul of Rabbi Shmuel bar Shilas. As there are levels of souls, so there are levels of places, from the Beis HaMikdash down to Shushan, the place of deepest concealment.

title.en: Shushan souls join Yerushalayim in Keser

summary.en: He tells the gathering that they are Shushan souls of the heel, and that through Purim Shushan merited to join Yerushalayim. Purim brings the level of Keser for a whole day, more than Shabbos, and Esther's request 'let them do tomorrow too' asks for that Keser.

title.en: Samuch v'nireh and mem-nun-tzadi-pei-chaf

summary.en: He brings the Gemara that a town near and visible from a walled city is judged like it, and the statement of the same Amora that the prophets established the final letters mem-nun-tzadi-pei-chaf, which were forgotten and re-established. Following the Bnei Yissaschar's question on what joins the two, he shows how the laws of walled cities for the Megillah parallel the walled cities of the Torah, with samuch v'nireh as the Megillah's chiddush.

title.en: Outside the camp, outside time, forgotten

summary.en: He explains that Amalek attacked those outside the cloud, and that we are souls of the heel for whom Hashem fights. Adar Sheni is outside time, the extra silver of the hooks was outside the count, and the last pesukim Moshe did not write and the halachos forgotten at his passing belong to souls of forgetting, from which Rabbi Akiva came.

title.en: Letters outside the alef-beis, souls outside the wall

summary.en: He brings the reversed alef-beis of Musaf Shabbos followed by mem-nun-tzadi-pei-chaf, letters of din, and explains that they are souls of forgetting that Keser lifts from the end to the beginning. This is the link to samuch v'nireh: Jews outside the wall who look toward Yerushalayim, whom Hashem on Purim brings inside the wall of fire, as mishloach manos carries each seudah out to another Jew.

title.en: Why Esther waited for tomorrow

summary.en: He asks why Esther put off her request to the next day when everyone was present, and answers that she knew the secret of Purim: Jews outside Yerushalayim must bind themselves to it, so she wanted two days of Purim. He begins the Maggid of Mezritch's teaching on the world of the golem.

title.en: The world of the golem and v'nahafoch hu

summary.en: He completes the Maggid's teaching that in the world of the golem everything can still be changed, and explains that Purim comes from there: Esther rose to it to turn Haman's two feasts into two days of Purim. He brings the Maharal that Purim must come as a reversal, and Bilaam's curse turned to blessing because Hashem loves the Jews.

title.en: The wine of Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the wine of Purim is a different kind of wine, as matzah eaten at the Seder is unlike matzah eaten afterward, and brings the Kedushas Levi that at the Purim seudah each bite and each drink should carry kabbalas ol malchus shamayim and simcha shel mitzvah.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Chanukah, the Mashgiach explains that the Greeks sought to abolish Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah, the foundations of Klal Yisrael, and that milah is the precondition for learning Torah as Hashem's heavenly Torah rather than as mere wisdom.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Rambam's words that the mitzvah of Chanukah is very dear, explaining that what a person sacrifices for becomes dear to him, as milah was dear to Avraham Avinu because of its pain. The Greeks decreed against Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah, the foundation of Klal Yisrael: without Rosh Chodesh there are no Yamim Tovim, which is why, as the Rambam says, Eretz Yisrael was never empty of Jews, and Shabbos heads the parsha of the Moadim. The Greeks valued wisdom and would allow Torah as reasoning, but not Torah from Sinai accepted even when not understood; for that, milah is the precondition, as in the Gemara's account of the Roman emperor's nephew. He closes by saying that Eliyahu Hanavi comes in person to a bris of parents who sacrifice for Torah, and blesses the child, named Avraham Yaakov after Rav Avraham Yaakov Pam.

en: What a person sacrifices himself for becomes dear to him, and so Chanukah, won through self-sacrifice, is a very dear mitzvah, as milah was dear to Avraham Avinu.
The Greeks sought to abolish Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah, the three mitzvos that are the foundation of Klal Yisrael.
Without Rosh Chodesh there are no Yamim Tovim and no existence for Klal Yisrael, and Shabbos is the head of the Moadim.
The Greeks accepted Torah as wisdom judged by reason, but milah is the precondition for learning Torah as Hashem's heavenly Torah from Sinai.
Eliyahu Hanavi comes in person to the bris of parents who are moser nefesh for Torah.

title.en: Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Chanukah is a dear mitzvah, comparing it to milah for Avraham Avinu, and lists the three mitzvos the Greeks wanted to abolish. He shows from the Rambam why Rosh Chodesh is the foundation of the Yamim Tovim and of Klal Yisrael's existence, and that Shabbos heads the Moadim.

title.en: Milah as the gateway to heavenly Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Greeks, lovers of wisdom, would allow Torah as reasoning but not as Hashem's Torah accepted even when not understood, which requires milah. He brings the Gemara about the Roman emperor's nephew who insisted on a bris to learn Torah, and the Greek decree that Jews write they have no portion in the G-d of Israel.

title.en: Eliyahu at this bris; blessings for the child

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Eliyahu Hanavi comes in person to important brisim and sends a messenger to others, and that he surely came to this bris of parents who are moser nefesh for Torah. He blesses the parents and the child, named Avraham Yaakov after Rav Avraham Yaakov Pam, that he should be worthy of the name.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that Purim reaches the lowest and most forgotten Jew: Hashem remembers every Jew, Mordechai finds merit in each one, and the seudah is a battle against Amalek, who wants to cut a Jew off from his Father in heaven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach calls the seudah the completion of Purim, a rectification of the Tree of Knowledge and a battle with Amalek, who wants to tear a Jew away from Hashem. On Purim every gate is open, as the Spinker Rebbe's story of a soul who always came too late shows, and Esther broke Haman's decree with mesirus nefesh. He explains Yehoshua's 'weakness' against Amalek and offers a chiddush: from ink left over from the last eight pesukim of the Torah, Moshe wrote the Megillah, the book of forgotten Jews. He then speaks of Achashverosh's rule, the lechem hapanim and parnassah, Mordechai who knew every language, the plunder decree and a story of R' Nachman of Breslov. He closes with Mordechai as a spark of Moshiach, hashgacha pratis, the night seudah and Yerushalayim, and the wine of Purim.

en: The Mashgiach says the Purim seudah is a war with Amalek, and its success depends on a Jew knowing that he will not let himself be torn away from his Father in heaven.
On Purim every gate is open and a Jew may enter even without permission, as Esther did; Haman's klipah is to make a Jew come too late.
The Megillah is the book of forgotten Jews: it assures that Hashem forgets no Jew, against Amalek who attaches himself to those who seem forgotten.
No Jewish letter is ever erased; at most some dirt clings to it and needs to be washed off.
Purim, rooted in 'ad delo yada' like the lechem hapanim that no one understands, is a source of parnassah.
Mordechai, 'doresh tov le'amo', is a spark of Moshiach who finds merit in even the worst Jew and tells him he has a Father in heaven.
Jews hold the main seudah at night, as Yerushalayim's Purim begins, to bind themselves to Yerushalayim and appease it.

title.en: The seudah as a battle with Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls the seudah the completion of Purim, a rectification of the Tree of Knowledge that atones even more than Yom Kippur. Purim is for the lowly, no sin separates a Jew from it, and the seudah is a battle with Amalek, who sows doubt about a Jew's pure neshamah.

title.en: The King comes down to His bride

summary.en: He compares today's darkness to the generation of the Flood, says that at the seudah one may ask for anything with truth, and brings 'lo me'astim' and the Zohar's parable of a king who goes into a foul-smelling place for his bride. The lower the descent, the higher the light that comes down.

title.en: March

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls for a march, and the assembly sings.

title.en: The soul who came too late

summary.en: On Purim one may enter the palace of any tzaddik, while Haman decreed that no one enters without permission. The Mashgiach tells of the Spinker Rebbe and a soul who always arrived at the heavenly palace of Purim just after Purim had ended.

title.en: Coming early and breaking through

summary.en: He asks why that soul was always late and answers that Amalek casts heaviness on a Jew so he comes late; one must come early to every mitzvah. The gate is still open until the last Jew finishes his Purim table, and as Esther broke through with mesirus nefesh, Hashem wants a Jew to break through to Him.

title.en: Mordechai's tefillah and Yehoshua's weakness

summary.en: From the Yismach Moshe: Mordechai knew the Megillah from Sinai and that the Jews would be saved, yet he davened as if he did not know, a level of a tzaddik. The Mashgiach reads 'vayachalosh Yehoshua' two ways and explains that Moshe told Yehoshua that wiping out Amalek is for Hashem in the days of Moshiach, which is why the Megillah will never be nullified.

title.en: 'Vesim be'oznei Yehoshua' and Moshe's ink

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that 'vezichram lo yasuf mizaram' equals 'vesim be'oznei Yehoshua' in gematria: the Megillah is for the future. He brings Chazal that Moshe's karnei hod came from ink left in his quill, and the question why extra ink was there, answered by the small aleph he wrote out of humility.

title.en: A chiddush: the Megillah from the leftover ink

summary.en: He offers a new idea: the last eight pesukim of the Torah carry the forgetting of Torah in the mourning for Moshe. Since Moshe did not write those pesukim, ink was left in his quill, and with it he wrote the Megillah, whose message is 'vezichram lo yasuf mizaram', that nothing be forgotten.

title.en: Forgotten Jews, Amalek and 'kol tokef'

summary.en: Every Jew is a letter in the Sefer Torah; forgotten Jews, like Shevet Dan at the back of the camp, belong to the eight pesukim outside what Moshe wrote. Amalek attaches himself to the forgotten, but Hashem forgets no Jew; the 1,700 halachos forgotten in the mourning for Moshe are hinted in 've'es ha'elef ushva me'os', and the Megillah's 'kol tokef' equals 1,700.

title.en: Why Achashverosh ruled the whole world

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Gemara stresses that Achashverosh ruled from one end of the world to the other. The purpose of creation is a dwelling for Hashem below, completed when Amalek is wiped out; mentioning a klipah in the words of Torah nullifies it, so writing Achashverosh into the Megillah nullifies the klipah of the whole world.

title.en: Memuchan and the lechem hapanim

summary.en: After candles for Mordechai and Esther are lit, the Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the seven officers stand for korbanos, and Memuchan, who brought Vashti's removal, for the lechem hapanim. He asks why the lechem hapanim had that power and answers that it is beyond understanding, as the Arizal's zemer and the Ramban show; the accuser is silenced when Jews do mitzvos they do not understand.

title.en: Purim and parnassah

summary.en: The lechem hapanim drew down parnassah, and R' Mottele Slonimer said every Jew needs eight hundred thousand gold coins. Haman's decree tried to take life and livelihood; Purim, rooted in 'ad delo yada' like the lechem hapanim, turned it around into parnassah, as the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov say, with gematrios on the eight hundred thousand coins.

title.en: Looking at Jews; Mordechai the master of languages

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Rebbe freed from Siberia who sat facing the people because he longed to see Jews; on Purim families gather to look at one another. Mordechai is called 'Bilshan' because he knew the languages of the nations, each a klipah, and on Purim he comes to every Jew to tell him not to be broken, that Hashem has not forgotten him.

title.en: No Jewish letter is erased

summary.en: Every Jew is pure, only Amalek stains him. The Mashgiach tells how the Lubavitcher Rebbe sent R' Yosef Weinberger to strengthen a grandson of a Jew who had helped him, and corrected him for saying that a straying Jew erases part of his letter in the Torah: a Jewish letter is never erased, only dirt clings to it.

title.en: Mordechai, Malachi and the seventy languages

summary.en: Because Mordechai knew the history in every language, he can reach every Jew. Rav Nachman's statement that Mordechai is Malachi links him to the last navi, who speaks until Eliyahu comes. Moshe explained the Torah in seventy languages, and Yosef, the first to go down to Egypt, had to know them to bring holiness into the exile; English, the last of them, now carries Gemara learning.

title.en: 'Gam alo' and the English-speaking generation

summary.en: Mordechai's 'dover shalom lechol zar'o' reaches the lowest levels of exile, even English. Hashem promised 'anochi a'alcha gam alo', which he shows equals America in gematria. Shushan, which sinned most at the feast, merited the Purim of Yerushalayim, and so the lowest Jew can reach the highest; our English-speaking generation will merit Moshiach.

title.en: The decree to plunder: a gift of parnassah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Haman also decreed to plunder Jewish money, and why Al Hanissim mentions it. Bringing the Ateres Yeshua's gematrios that the Megillah is a segulah for parnassah, he answers that Hashem let the decree be made so that, once overturned, it would become parnassah for Jews.

title.en: Adar as a fence: fixed times and bitachon

summary.en: From the Gemara and Rashi on the adar plant that grows into a wall, the Mashgiach teaches that Adar is a time of bitachon: a Jew should set a fixed wall of time for Torah and not cross it for business, since no one touches what is prepared for another. The Jews did not take the spoils, showing their trust in Hashem.

title.en: R' Nachman's merchant and the book of parnassah

summary.en: The Mashgiach retells a story of R' Nachman of Breslov: a merchant lost a precious find at sea, kept his composure and told the ship's captain nothing, and in the end the captain's goods came to him. What is written for a Jew in the book of parnassah will be his, which is why the Jews did not touch the spoils. He ends by calling a grandson to dance.

title.en: Mordechai: a Father in heaven

summary.en: The Arizal says Mordechai's soul is from Yesod Abba; in plain terms, Mordechai laid the foundation that we have a Father in heaven. Mordechai is a spark of Moshiach who finds merit in the worst Jew; the last pasuk of the Megillah, 'doresh tov le'amo', is for the lowest, and Mordechai throws a rope to every Jew drowning in despair.

title.en: The Megillah as a lesson in hashgacha pratis

summary.en: Every detail of the Megillah turns out to be part of the miracle, and so is everything that happens in the world. The Mashgiach brings the Ramban on hidden miracles and the words of the Sfas Emes: one who has emunah and bitachon knows that all Hashem does with him is the greatest good, and Purim is the time to fix this emunah in oneself.

summary.en: Hashem, who set fire to Tziyon, will rebuild it with fire. Though the poskim cry out to eat the main seudah by day, Jews hold it at night, when Purim begins in Yerushalayim, to bind themselves to it, as a rectification for the feast of Achashverosh that celebrated Yerushalayim not being rebuilt. The Mashgiach speaks of Hashem's right hand held back, Mordechai 'ish Yemini' and Amalek's war on the right hand.

summary.en: Near chatzos the Mashgiach speaks of the wine of Purim: like an esrog whose value is its mitzvah, the wine holds Hashem's kingship over the whole world, unlike the revealed miracles of Pesach night. He asks that Purim be carried through the year, blesses all Jews, and says Purim, greater than Yom Kippur, now rises up into Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: At the Purim seudah the Mashgiach teaches that Purim, and above all the Yerushalayim Purim of the second day, binds the Jews to Yerushalayim and to the days of Moshiach, repairing Achashverosh's feast that celebrated the end of the hope for the Beis Hamikdash.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that the seudah is a longing for Yerushalayim. Achashverosh made his feast after calculating that the seventy years had passed, and the Jews who came were guilty of a great chillul Hashem; Mordechai, the 'Ish Yemini' from Binyamin, belongs to Yerushalayim. He tells how Reb Yitzchak of Vorka called 'Yidelach, come to me', and says the whole Megillah calls this out, as Moshiach will. Matanos la'evyonim show that Jews are Hashem's children, and their money must carry fire, unlike Haman's cold silver. He explains why Mordechai, a complete tzaddik, needed a share in the people's trouble to help them. He shows that the Megillah was written with ruach hakodesh, seen in Heaven, and is the Megillah of the days of Moshiach. Esther asked for a second, Yerushalayim Purim. Finally he tells how Achashverosh carried a spark of Rabbi Yochanan ben Torasa, and closes with l'chaim for Yerushalayim.

en: The Mashgiach says the Purim seudah is a longing for Yerushalayim, and that those gathered are binding themselves to it.
The whole Megillah calls out 'Yidelach, come to me', the call of Moshiach, who will draw every Jew close.
Hashem wants the fire of love inside the money a Jew gives, not the money itself; this is the 'full silver' that Haman's cold money lacked.
A tzaddik who stands apart from the people cannot shield them, so Mordechai needed a share in their trouble for his tefillos to help.
The Megillah was seen written in Heaven, and it speaks in its hidden sense of the days of Moshiach, which is why it will remain when the other books of the Prophets and Writings are nullified.
Esther asked for a second day of Purim for Yerushalayim alone, a Purim of the days of Moshiach.
Achashverosh carried a spark of holiness, the soul of Rabbi Yochanan ben Torasa, and through it merited that Purim came about through him.

title.en: Daniel's reckoning and 'Ish Yemini'

summary.en: He notes that even Daniel took the reckoning seriously. He then asks why Mordechai, whose mother was from Yehuda, is called 'Ish Yemini', and connects it to Binyamin, in whose portion the Beis Hamikdash stood.

title.en: Mordechai belongs to Yerushalayim

summary.en: Binyamin stands for Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim, so by calling himself 'Ish Yemini' Mordechai declares that in exile his heart is in Yerushalayim. The Mashgiach says those gathered at the seudah have come to bind themselves to Yerushalayim.

title.en: 'Yidelach, come to me'

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Kotzker once drove his chassidim away and Reb Yitzchak of Vorka stood on a bench and called them to him. Today, in a time of hester panim, Jews must be drawn close; Adar is a time of closeness, and Purim, like Moshiach, calls every Jew near.

title.en: Matanos la'evyonim and the burning love in money

summary.en: He asks why Purim has matanos la'evyonim and answers with Rabbi Akiva's reply to Turnus Rufus that Jews are Hashem's children. Then he asks what Rashi's 'explanation of the money' means, and brings the Alshich: Hashem wants the burning love inside the money.

title.en: Haman's cold money and the fire in 'kesef malei'

summary.en: Haman's ten thousand talents were cold, frozen money. Avraham Avinu and Dovid HaMelech paid 'kesef malei', and the Mashgiach shows that the filled-out letters of 'kesef' add up to 'esh', fire, which is also the difference between Yisrael and Amalek. Hashem told Haman to keep his money.

summary.en: Singing.

title.en: Knesses Yisrael's complaint against Dovid

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Knesses Yisrael complained against Dovid for not killing Shimi, from whom Mordechai descended, and against Shaul for sparing Agag. Following the Kehillas Yaakov, Knesses Yisrael is the Shechinah, and he asks how it could complain when without Mordechai there would be no Purim.

title.en: Why a complete tzaddik cannot shield others

summary.en: He brings the Gemara about a plague that spared Rav's neighborhood not in Rav's merit, and the Yismach Moshe's explanation: a complete tzaddik is outside the decree and so cannot save those under it. Moshe Rabbeinu broke the luchos to share in the people's sin so he could daven for them.

title.en: The Belzer Rav and Mordechai: being part of the people

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Belzer Rav, who asked for news in the mikveh and arrived in Eretz Yisrael without his beard, to be part of the Jewish people. So too the Shechinah's complaint that Mordechai provoked Haman gave him a share in the people's trouble, and then his tefillos could be accepted.

title.en: The Megillah written with ruach hakodesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's proofs that the Megillah was written with ruach hakodesh, and Shmuel's proof from 'kiymu v'kiblu', which alone cannot be refuted. He asks how Shmuel could say that had he been there he would have said something better than the Tannaim.

title.en: Accepting the Megillah into Kesuvim; Rabbi Meir's Sefer Torah

summary.en: He brings the Yerushalmi that the elders hesitated to accept the Megillah until Hashem enlightened their eyes to find it hinted in the word 'basefer'. Then he brings the Gemara that a Sefer Torah may not be written from memory, yet Rabbi Meir did so, and asks why.

title.en: The fiery Torah in Heaven

summary.en: The Hafla'ah answers that the Torah is written in Heaven in black fire on white fire, and Rabbi Meir copied from there. His teachers could certainly see the Megillah written in Heaven, and so knew it was ruach hakodesh. The Yaaros Devash explains how Mordechai's words show the Megillah was dictated from Heaven.

title.en: The Megillah of the days of Moshiach

summary.en: The Megillah is more than a story of the past: the Yerushalmi and the Rambam say it will remain when the other books of the Prophets and Writings are nullified. The Mashgiach explains that its hidden meaning speaks of the days of Moshiach, where 'Achashverosh' means the Ribono shel Olam.

title.en: What the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah saw

summary.en: Only one who knew the secret of the days of Moshiach could accept the Megillah, so Hashem enlightened the eyes of the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah and they saw it in Heaven. This is what Shmuel understood: the Tannaim had seen it in Heaven and out of humility brought proofs from pesukim.

title.en: Mantzepach: Purim seen in Heaven

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Tosafos that the letters mantzepach were revealed by the 'tzofim', the seers, and shows that 'kol tzofayich' is in gematria Purim: they saw Purim and the Megillah in Heaven.

title.en: Esther's second day: a Yerushalayim Purim

summary.en: The Megillah has a plain meaning and a hidden one. Esther asked for a second day of Purim for Yerushalayim alone, a different kind of Purim belonging to the days of Moshiach; 'gam machar la'Yehudim' equals 'Dovid ben Yishai' in gematria.

title.en: Dovid, Yerushalayim, and how Purim reaches down

summary.en: Dovid is part of Yerushalayim. The Mashgiach brings from the Arizal that Purim's keser holiness lasts the whole day, and from Torah Or that what is higher at its root reaches lower; so Purim belongs above all to the lowest Jews, those who stumbled.

title.en: Two sins and two days of Purim

summary.en: The Jews sinned by bowing to the image and by enjoying Achashverosh's feast, which denied the coming of the Beis Hamikdash. The Mashgiach suggests the first day of Purim answers the first sin and the second, Yerushalayim's day, answers the sin against the building of Yerushalayim.

title.en: Not forgetting Yerushalayim

summary.en: Through teshuvah the Jews of Shushan merited a Yerushalayim Purim, the Purim of Moshiach. Tonight, he says, we bind ourselves to the Jews of Yerushalayim and fulfil 'im eshkachech Yerushalayim'; Mordechai, the man of Binyamin, is the man of Yerushalayim. He ends with l'chaim.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Singing.

title.en: The kallah's twenty-four ornaments

summary.en: Rashi compares the twenty-four books of Tanach to a kallah's twenty-four ornaments, which the Mashgiach links to the permutations of the Name of Adnus. Knesses Yisrael is the kallah and Hashem the chassan; Shir Hashirim is the song of chassan and kallah, and Purim is their Yom Tov.

title.en: Esther's book as the kallah's crown

summary.en: Esther wanted her book to be the finest ornament, the crown jewel completing the twenty-four. The sages hesitated to accept it while Amalek was not yet wiped out, wishing to wait for Moshiach; but the whole matter of Moshiach is already in the Megillah.

title.en: Letters of redemption and the five reading days

summary.en: He brings the Avnei Nezer that the letters mantzepach stand for five redemptions, the tzadi for Moshiach, matching the five days on which the Megillah can be read, so that Shushan Purim is the final redemption. Purim reaches the lowest Jews first, and the Megillah, crown of the kallah, is Yerushalayim's joy.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Singing.

title.en: How Achashverosh became king

summary.en: The Gemara says Achashverosh made himself king, while the Chasam Sofer brings that he was the son of the king of Persia. He resolves it with the rotation between Madai and Paras: it was Madai's turn, so he paid to reign. Everything in the Megillah is told for the good of the Jews.

title.en: Paras, Yishmael and the Megillah in every generation

summary.en: Yishmael is the harshest exile, and Paras is bound up with Yishmael. The Megillah applies in every generation: Paras today is Iran, where again someone openly speaks of destroying the Jews. Just as Achashverosh turned around, so the Megillah speaks of our own time.

title.en: The cow that rested on Shabbos

summary.en: Asking what merit Achashverosh had to do good for the Jews, the Mashgiach tells the story of a cow that would not work on Shabbos, which led its gentile owner to convert and become Rabbi Yochanan ben Torasa. From Gilgulei Neshamos he brings that Achashverosh came back in that convert and Vashti in the cow.

title.en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Torasa and the spark in Achashverosh

summary.en: Achashverosh's feast spread despair of Moshiach; as Rabbi Yochanan ben Torasa he repaired this by telling Rabbi Akiva that Bar Kochva was not Moshiach, sparing the Jews a crisis of faith. That spark of holiness in Achashverosh is why he paid to become king and why Purim came through him.

title.en: Esther's wine and l'chaim for Yerushalayim

summary.en: An esrog is cheap all year but precious on Sukkos because of the holy names resting in it; so too the wine, 'yayin hameshumar', equals Esther in gematria. The Mashgiach calls to drink l'chaim to Yerushalayim and blesses those present.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: Poorly recorded stretch.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Singing at the end of the seudah.

oneLiner.en: At a bris the day after Parshas Balak was read, the Mashgiach explains that the greater the kedushah, the thicker the orla that covers it, in the body, in Eretz Yisrael, in Balak who hid the spark of Moshiach, and in the Three Weeks, and that the mitzvah of milah reveals the hidden holiness.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by asking why the wicked Balak has a sedra named after him, while Nechemia, who built the second Beis Hamikdash, did not merit a sefer under his own name, because he said 'remember me for good'. He adds that the recent printing of a separate Sefer Nechemia is a message for our generation: in a time of great difficulty, a Jew must find the good in himself and take heart from his progress. Returning to Balak, he explains that Moshiach descends from Balak through Rus, so Balak's soul held a holy spark that his klipah tried to keep captive. The rule is that the greater the kedushah, the thicker the shell: the orla in the body, the wicked nations in Eretz Yisrael, and the mourning of the Three Weeks in time. Pinchas, who follows Balak, is the angel of the bris. The bris, he concludes, awakens Hashem to perform the great milah of the whole world.

en: Nechemia's sefer is not called by his name because he stressed his own accomplishment, yet today the printed Sefer Nechemia tells our generation to search out its own good points.
Balak merits a sedra because Moshiach descends from him through Rus; the name refers to the holy spark inside him, not to his shell.
The greater the kedushah, the thicker the klipah that covers it.
The pattern repeats in space, time and soul: the orla over the holiest part of the body, the worst nations over Eretz Yisrael, and the mourning of the Three Weeks over the holiest days of the year.
Pinchas, read after Balak, is the angel of the bris who removed the klipah of Zimri and revealed the holiness of Klal Yisrael.
Hashem acts like a shadow of Klal Yisrael: performing the mitzvah of milah awakens Him to remove the orla from the whole world.

title.en: Balak's sedra and Nechemia's missing sefer

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Balak has a sedra named after him while Nechemia, because he said 'remember me for good', did not get a sefer under his name. He explains that the recent printing of a separate Sefer Nechemia is a message for our difficult generation: to find the good in oneself, give oneself credit and take comfort in one's progress.

title.en: The spark of Moshiach hidden in Balak

summary.en: The Mashgiach traces Moshiach's lineage from Balak through Rus to David Hamelech, and explains that Balak tried to keep this holy spark captive inside his klipah. Through the name Ben Tzippor and the AtBash of Balak's letters, he shows that the sedra's name refers to the hidden inner Balak.

title.en: The greater the kedushah, the thicker the orla

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the holiest soul was covered by Balak's hideous shell, and answers that great kedushah is always covered by a great klipah: the orla over the holiest part of the body, the worst nations over Eretz Yisrael. He then brings Pinchas, the angel of the bris who removed the klipah of Zimri, and the three dimensions of space, time and soul.

title.en: The orla over the Three Weeks

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the rule to time: the Three Weeks are holy days of Moshiach covered by the orla of mourning. He tells how the Plantcher Rebbe once held an empty cup on Tisha B'Av and acted out the Kiddush that will be made when Moshiach comes, and he ties the 22 days to the days from Rosh Hashanah to Simchas Torah.

title.en: This bris and the great milah of the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises those present who removed the orla from themselves, and explains that Hashem acts like a shadow: the mitzvah of milah awakens Him to remove the orla from the whole world. He closes with brachos for the parents and the child and for the coming of Eliyahu and Moshiach.

oneLiner.en: At his Purim seudah the Mashgiach shows Purim as a day above the world, when Hashem's closeness reaches even the lowest Jew, the disguises of the Megillah and of the world fall away, and Yerushalayim and its Beis Hamikdash are honored and rebuilt.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the uniqueness of Purim, a day borrowed from the world of tikkun, and with Rabbi Masna's petichta, 'Elokim kerovim elav': Hashem loves and hears even the lowest Jew, and Purim, the lowest of the festivals, is bound to the fiftieth gate. He explains Shushan Purim as an honor for Yerushalayim and a lesson in unity. Through Memuchan, identified with Daniel, he ties Purim to parnassah and tzedakah. He contrasts the Megillah's story with its inner layer, where the king is Hashem, and explains why it is read twice. He then shows how Moshe's new birth at the fiftieth gate defeated Haman, how Sarah's merit and Esther's revelation led to the building of the Beis Hamikdash, and how a spark from Shlomo passed through Vashti and Achashverosh to its tikkun, closing with Purim wine and blessings.

en: Purim belongs to the world of tikkun; that is why the Megillah will remain when the other books of Nevi'im and Kesuvim are nullified.
Purim reveals that Hashem chose and loves every Jew, even the lowest, and listens when he calls to Him.
Shushan Purim is an honor for Yerushalayim, and its greatest honor is that Chazal derived it through their derashos.
The essence of Purim is unity: all Jews are one family, joined by the seudah and mishloach manos.
The Megillah has an inner layer in which the king is Hashem, and in the future it will be learned that way.
On Purim every Jew reaches the fiftieth gate, where no blemish reaches, and is born anew.
All a Jew sees in the world is a garment; one dresses up on Purim because the whole world is a disguise covering Hashem.

candidateTopics: building of the second beis hamikdash

title.en: Haman's boast and the uniqueness of Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens the seudah with Haman's boast that only he was invited to Esther's feast. He cites the Ma'or VaShemesh that there is no day in the year like Purim, a day borrowed from the future, and explains that the Megillah will remain when the other books of Nevi'im and Kesuvim are nullified because it belongs to the world of tikkun.

title.en: Shushan Purim, Shabbos and the eis ratzon

summary.en: He explains that Shushan Purim leads into Shabbos, which can only add good, so Purim remains. The seudah is a great eis ratzon: one who accepts the Torah anew with longing, as at 'kiymu vekiblu', can ask for every good, as tzaddikim brought salvations on Purim. He then turns to the Gemara's petichtos to the Megillah and Rabbi Masna's passuk.

title.en: Rabbi Masna's petichta: Hashem is close

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Rabbi Masna's petichta lacks the usual opening words, and explains that Purim shows how Hashem loves even the lowest Jew. He brings the Chasam Sofer that the salvation was prepared even while Jews sinned at Achashverosh's feast, and concludes that Rabbi Masna's words are not a key to Purim but Purim itself.

title.en: Modeh Ani and Purim at the lowest level

summary.en: He brings the custom to say Modeh Ani before washing the hands, since no impurity touches a Jew's Modeh Ani. Chanukah and Purim correspond to the lowest levels, yet Purim at the end of the year is the Modeh Ani of the Jewish people, the end bound to the beginning, Adar to Nissan. Purim and Yom Kippur share the level of 'lifnei Hashem', above the names.

title.en: Near and far: the fiftieth gate

summary.en: He continues that the fiftieth gate, alluded to in 'lifnei Hashem tit'haru', is a place no blemish reaches, like the Kodesh HaKodashim. On Purim a Jew should reflect how far he is from Hashem and yet how near, as Mordechai wrote to 'the near and the far'.

title.en: Shushan Purim: an honor for Yerushalayim

summary.en: Now it is night and Purim has begun in Yerushalayim. The Mashgiach asks why Esther requested another day and why it follows the walled cities. Since Achashverosh's feast celebrated that Yerushalayim would not be rebuilt, a day was set to honor it, and its greatest honor is that Shushan Purim is not written in the pesukim but derived by Chazal. On Purim, unlike other Yamim Tovim, a person follows the place where he is.

title.en: Unity and the repair of the moon

summary.en: A visitor keeps Purim with the people of the place because Purim's essence is unity: all Jews are one family, bound by the seudah and mishloach manos. The moon's diminishing came from a lack of unity; Esther, likened to the moon, repairs it, and 'hayoshvim be'arei haprazos' is in gematria the repair of the moon's blemish.

title.en: Memuchan and the lechem hapanim

summary.en: The Gemara reads the names of Achashverosh's seven princes as names of korbanos, Memuchan corresponding to the lechem hapanim. The Chasam Sofer explains that the officials below share names with the angels above, so their names arouse the merit of the korbanos. The Gemara identifies Memuchan with Haman, yet Tosafos brings a Midrash that he is Daniel, and the Mashgiach asks why.

title.en: The Maharal's question and Daniel's vision

summary.en: Tosafos was answering the Maharal's question: since the miracle began with Vashti's removal through Memuchan, how did Haman merit to start it? If Memuchan is Daniel, the question falls away, but why did Daniel push to speak first? He turns to Daniel chapter 10, where Daniel alone sees the vision, and ends with the teaching that the table brings parnassah, so the miracle began from the lechem hapanim.

title.en: Purim, parnassah and the souls of Dan

summary.en: Purim and all of Adar bring parnassah, with gematrias from the Ateres Yeshua. Daniel, the first point of the miracle, was shown the end of days because his soul reached down to the last souls before Moshiach; Purim at the end of the year corresponds to those souls, to Dan, whom Amalek attacked, and Daniel's name is bound to Dan.

title.en: Tzedakah before Moshiach; Daniel speaks first as Memuchan

summary.en: The Tanya teaches that before Moshiach one must rely above all on tzedakah. Daniel risked himself advising Nevuchadnetzar to give tzedakah, the Rambam writes that no joy is greater than gladdening the poor, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani told the people to pray about the famine. So Daniel, as Memuchan, the lechem hapanim, spoke first to annul the decree by arousing parnassah for the Jews; 'Ani Daniel' is in gematria Memuchan, the prophet of parnassah and gifts to the poor.

title.en: Why the Megillah is read twice

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Megillah is read at night and again by day, when every Torah reading is read once. He brings the Yerushalmi, cited by the Rambam, that the Megillah will remain when the Nevi'im and Kesuvim are nullified, and asks what makes Mordechai greater than Yeshayahu, pointing to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proof and the Chasam Sofer's words that through the Megillah the Torah was accepted with love.

title.en: The two layers of the Megillah

summary.en: He describes hearing the Satmar Rav read the Megillah: one heard a different Megillah. The Megillah has two layers, the story learned in cheder and an inner layer in which the king is Hashem; at his Purim seudah the Satmar Rav once said he saw neither Mordechai nor Haman, only the Ribono shel Olam. So it is read twice, once to understand and once with emunah, for it holds what cannot be understood.

title.en: The chen of the Megillah; Thursday night and Shabbos

summary.en: The Megillah, like Esther, carries a chen that cannot be grasped, a thread of kindness given to strengthen the weakest Jews in exile, the stragglers of Dan whom Amalek attacks. After singing, he speaks of the custom to gather on Thursday night with Shabbos niggunim; Purim too has the holiness of Shabbos, and tonight the two come together.

title.en: Zemiros

summary.en: Singing of Shabbos zemiros.

title.en: Why Haman did not know Moshe was born in Adar

summary.en: Haman rejoiced that his lot fell in Adar, the month Moshe died, not knowing he was also born then. The Mashgiach asks how he could compute one and not the other, and explains that Moshe attained forty-nine gates of understanding and did not pass on the fiftieth, which is above the world. Mordechai, a spark of Moshe, received the Torah anew; Haman sought the fiftieth gate of impurity to overpower him but could not reach it alone.

title.en: Moshe's new birth and the fiftieth gate

summary.en: Through Zeresh, since in impurity the female is stronger, as the Ohr HaChaim writes, Haman built a fifty-amah gallows. The Shelah writes that on the day of his passing Moshe reached the fiftieth gate, which is like a new birth; Haman did not know this because Moshe never taught it. On Purim every Jew reaches that gate and is born anew, 'ani hayom yelidticha', and should become a new Jew.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: A few words on the joy of Purim, then singing.

title.en: 'On that day': up to half the kingdom

summary.en: He asks why the Megillah stresses 'on that day' the king gave Haman's house to Esther, when the Midrash says that money built the second Beis Hamikdash. Achashverosh offered Esther up to half the kingdom but not the Beis Hamikdash, since Yerushalayim, the center of the world, would rival his rule. By the Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer he ruled 252 provinces, and losing half for blocking the building should have left him 126.

title.en: Sarah's merit and Achashverosh's reasoning

summary.en: Esther ruled 127 provinces in the merit of Sarah's 127 years, so eleven extra remained. Achashverosh reasoned that had he been punished for the Beis Hamikdash, Yerushalayim would have been taken first; since he even had extra provinces, the loss was not for that, so he made a feast. He did not know Esther was Jewish.

title.en: Esther's revelation and the building of the Beis Hamikdash

summary.en: On the day Esther revealed she was a Jewish child, a granddaughter of Sarah, Achashverosh grasped the truth, took fright and gave the money to build the Beis Hamikdash. 'Vatischak leyom acharon', Avraham's eulogy for Sarah, alludes to Adar, the day of the last Jews, of Dan. He speaks of the state of the world before the geulah and closes with a blessing to be together in Yerushalayim.

title.en: Adir Hu

summary.en: Singing of Adir Hu.

title.en: Longing for Yerushalayim; Shilo and the open city

summary.en: Shushan Purim in Yerushalayim expresses the Jews' hope and longing for it, and Jews abroad rejoice with it. Following the Pri Tzaddik's rule that every Gemara passage relates to its Mishnah, he links the Megillah's derashos to the Mishnah comparing Shilo to Yerushalayim: Shilo had no wall for kodashim kalim. In the future Yerushalayim will spread out without walls, as Zechariah saw the angel stopped from measuring it.

title.en: Yerushalayim without walls

summary.en: Every Jew has a place in his heart for Yerushalayim, and on Shushan Purim even those outside the wall enter it; where a Jew's thoughts are, there he is, says the Ba'al Shem Tov. The closed mem and the letters of din give the other side a hold, but in the future Yerushalayim will have no wall. Shushan, whose Jews sinned at the feast, keeps Yerushalayim's laws; Esther regained the Shechinah by turning toward Yerushalayim, as every Jew does in davening.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Singing.

title.en: At the end everything will be understood

summary.en: After singing, the Mashgiach reads 'vehaya be'acharis hayamim nachon yihyeh' as 'at the end everything will be right'. The Megillah is hester, as Chazal find Esther in 'haster astir'; the greatness of Achashverosh and Haman is concealment, but at the end all questions will be answered, and the Megillah's opening alludes to this.

title.en: The world in disguise

summary.en: In the deeper reading the klipos of the Megillah are holy names. The five Chumashim are clothed in the Megillah, like Binyamin's five changes of clothes. All a Jew sees is a garment; that is why one dresses up on Purim, and an honest Jew tears off the disguise to see only Hashem. He brings the Midrash in which Haman claims Mordechai's grandfather bowed to his, and the Zohar that Yaakov bowed to the Shechinah.

title.en: Mordechai the Yehudi

summary.en: The Shechinah stood between Yaakov and Esav, which explains Mordechai's answer, 'ki higid lahem asher hu Yehudi': the name Yehudi holds Hashem's Name with the Jew standing at its side. 'King Achashverosh' alludes to Hashem, first and last, and at the end of days the disguises will fall away, 'velo yikanef od morecha'.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Singing.

title.en: Purim Torah: the vavs in Achashverosh's name

summary.en: Calling it Purim Torah, the Mashgiach notes that Achashverosh's name begins with two vavs, later has one, and at the end of the Megillah has none. From the Shalsheles HaKabbalah he brings that Nevuchadnetzar descended from Shlomo HaMelech and the Queen of Sheba, and that Shlomo drank no wine during the seven years he built the Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: Shlomo's sleep at the dedication

summary.en: On the night of the dedication Shlomo drank wine and slept late, the Tamid could not be offered on time, and a decree of destruction followed; Yirmiyahu, a gilgul of Shlomo, saw it. The Mashgiach asks how Shlomo, whose love for Hashem had no equal and who was zealous in building, could oversleep, and answers that a hidden spark of Nevuchadnetzar was in him.

title.en: The spark passes to Vashti and Achashverosh

summary.en: When holiness grows strong the other side fights with all its force, and the spark made Shlomo sleep. It passed to Vashti, who would not let Achashverosh build the Beis Hamikdash. Just as the Ohr HaChaim says a holy spark of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon was drawn out of Shechem, Achashverosh drew this spark from Vashti, a spark of sleep that would come to its tikkun.

title.en: The king could not sleep; the Beis Hamikdash is built

summary.en: The spark that made Shlomo sleep now kept Achashverosh awake, 'nadedah shenas hamelech', and led to the building of the Beis Hamikdash with Haman's money. A person's possessions are part of his soul, as with Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey, so the spark passed into Haman's estate and from it into the Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: The vavs freed; the great tikkunim of Purim

summary.en: A name missing a letter of Hashem's Name signals the other side; Achashverosh's vavs were sparks of holiness that left him step by step. He tells the Midrash of the cow that would not work on Shabbos and the gentile who converted, Yochanan ben Torsa, who per the Gilgulei Neshamos was a gilgul of Achashverosh. Purim brings great tikkunim, and a Jew who longs to be erlich can take hold of its power.

title.en: Niggun

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks briefly about the seudah, then a niggun.

title.en: Purim wine

summary.en: At the time of a mitzvah its object holds holy names: an esrog worth little before Sukkos costs hundreds during it, and Shabbos wine differs from weekday wine. Purim wine is another wine altogether, 'yayin hameshumar', in gematria Esther. He distinguishes being ongetrunken on Purim from being drunk, and blesses that the Megillah, the gifts, mishloach manos and the seudah stand by us all our lives.

title.en: Blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach blesses those present with success in spiritual and material matters, parnassah, shidduchim and refuah, and a kosher Pesach in Yerushalayim; then a niggun.

title.en: Closing niggun

summary.en: Singing.
